# Calcium channel blockers

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Relevant pharmacology > Calcium channel blockers*

[Original Article Link](/library/cm0aeg)

---

## Summary

<u>Calcium</u> channel blockers (CCBs) are drugs that bind to and block L-type <u>calcium</u> channels, which are the predominant <u>calcium</u> channels in the <u>myocardium</u> and vascular <u>smooth muscles</u>. By blocking these channels, CCBs cause peripheral arterial <u>vasodilation</u> (leading to a drop in blood pressure) and <u>myocardial</u> <u>depression</u> (leading to negative <u>chronotropic</u>, <u>inotropic</u>, and <u>dromotropic</u> effects on the <u>myocardium</u>). CCBs are classified into two major groups according to the main site of action: <u>Dihydropyridines</u> (e.g., <u>nifedipine</u>, <u>amlodipine</u>) are potent <u>vasodilators</u>, and <u>nondihydropyridines</u> (e.g., <u>verapamil</u>) are potent <u>myocardial</u> depressants. <u>Diltiazem</u>, a common nondihydropyridine, has moderate <u>vasodilatory</u> and <u>myocardial</u> depressant effects. <u>Nondihydropyridines</u> are also categorized as class IV <u>antiarrhythmic drugs</u> and are used in the treatment of <u>supraventricular arrhythmias</u>. The most common indications for CCB use are <u>arterial hypertension</u> and <u>stable angina</u>. The main side effects of <u>dihydropyridines</u> are caused by <u>vasodilation</u> (e.g., <u>headache</u>, <u>peripheral edema</u>); those of <u>nondihydropyridines</u> are caused by <u>myocardial</u> <u>depression</u> (e.g., <u>bradyarrhythmias</u>, <u>atrioventricular block</u>). CCBs are contraindicated in patients with preexisting cardiac conduction disorders, symptomatic <u>hypotension</u>, and/or <u>acute coronary syndrome</u>.




See also “<u>Calcium channel blocker poisoning</u>.”

## Pharmacodynamics

* CCBs bind to and block <u>L-type calcium channels</u> in cardiac and vascular <u>smooth muscle cells</u>;   → decreased frequency of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> channel opening in response to <u>cell membrane</u> <u>depolarization</u>;   → decreased transmembrane <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> current

* Effects of decreased <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> influx

* Vascular <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation;   → <u>vasodilation</u> → decreased peripheral <u>vascular resistance</u> → decreased <u>afterload</u> → decreased blood pressure

* Decreased <u>cardiac muscle</u> contractility (negative <u>inotropic</u> action) → decreased <u>cardiac output</u> → decreased blood pressure

* Decreased <u>SA node</u> discharge rate (negative <u>chronotropic</u> action);   → decreased <u>heart rate</u> (<u>bradycardia</u>) → decreased <u>cardiac output</u> → decreased blood pressure

* Decreased <u>AV node</u> conduction (negative <u>dromotropic</u> action) → termination of <u>supraventricular arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Dihydropyridines</u> act mainly on vascular <u>smooth muscle</u>. The order of <u>potency</u> is <u>nifedipine</u>/<u>amlodipine</u> followed by the <u>nondihydropyridines</u> <u>verapamil</u> and <u>diltiazem</u>.

* <u>Nondihydropyridines</u> act mainly on the <u>heart</u>. The order of <u>potency</u> is <u>verapamil</u> > <u>diltiazem</u> > <u>amlodipine</u>/<u>nifedipine</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Dihydropyridine CCBs</u> (<u>nifedipine</u> and <u>amlodipine</u>) primarily act on vascular <u>smooth muscles</u>. <u>Nondihydropyridine CCBs</u> (<u>verapamil</u> > <u>diltiazem</u>) primarily act on the <u>heart</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Verapamil mainly acts on Ventricles and Amlodipine mainly acts on Arteries.

## Indications

### All CCBs [[4]](/library/i7YJlq)




* Arterial <u>hypertension</u> (esp. <u>amlodipine</u> )

* <u>Stable angina</u>: for patients with <u>contraindications for beta blockers</u> or who are not responsive to <u>beta blockers</u>

* <u>Vasospastic angina</u> (<u>Prinzmetal angina</u>)

* <u>Achalasia</u>

* <u>Diffuse esophageal spasm</u>





### <u>Dihydropyridines</u>




* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u> (e.g., <u>nifedipine</u>, <u>felodipine</u>)

* <u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>;  (e.g., <u>nimodipine</u>; , <u>nicardipine</u>) to prevent secondary vasospasm

* <u>Tocolysis</u>

* <u>Gestational hypertension</u>

* <u>Hypertensive urgency</u>/<u>hypertensive emergency</u> (e.g., <u>nicardipine</u>, <u>clevidipine</u>)

* <u>Thromboangiitis obliterans</u>





### <u>Nondihydropyridines</u>




* <u>Supraventricular arrhythmias</u> (<u>verapamil</u> and <u>diltiazem</u> ; )

* <u>Supraventricular tachycardia</u>

* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>atrial flutter</u>

* <u>Cardiomyopathy</u> (<u>hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy</u>, <u>restrictive cardiomyopathy</u>)

* <u>Migraine</u>

* <u>Verapamil</u>: <u>cluster headache</u>





> [!TIP]
> Short-acting CCBs (e.g., <u>nifedipine</u>) are not indicated for monotherapy of <u>angina</u> because they cause <u>hypotension</u> and secondary <u>reflex tachycardia</u>, which can worsen cardiac <u>ischemia</u>.

---

## Adverse effects

### <u>Dihydropyridines</u> [[5]](/library/6Oajtk)[[6]](/library/KOaUtk)




* Effects due to <u>vasodilation</u>

* Peripheral <u>edema</u>;  (esp. <u>amlodipine</u>):  can be reduced by adding a <u>renin-angiotensin system</u> <u>antagonist</u> (<u>ACEI</u> or <u>ARB</u>).

* <u>Headaches</u>, <u>dizziness</u>

* <u>Facial flushing</u>, feeling of warmth

* Reflex tachycardia: a condition of <u>tachycardia</u> secondary to a decrease in blood pressure (esp. <u>nifedipine</u>)

* <u>Vasodilation</u> lowers the blood pressure, which stimulates <u>baroreceptors</u> of the <u>sympathetic nervous system</u>, resulting in <u>reflex tachycardia</u>. [[7]](/library/JOastk)

* May worsen symptoms of <u>angina</u>

* <u>Gingival hyperplasia</u>





> [!TIP]
> Due to their <u>vasodilatory</u> effects, <u>dihydropyridines</u> should be considered in the <u>differential diagnosis of peripheral edema</u>.




### <u>Nondihydropyridines</u> [[6]](/library/KOaUtk)




* Benzothiazepines: similar to those of the other CCB classes, but milder

* <u>Phenylalkylamines</u>

* Reduced contractility

* <u>Bradycardia</u>

* <u>AV block</u>  [[8]](/library/pOaLtk)

* <u>Gingival hyperplasia</u>

* <u>Verapamil</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>

* <u>Hyperprolactinemia</u>  [[9]](/library/APXRhy)





We list the most important adverse effects. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Contraindications

### All CCBs [[10]](/library/I_0Ypi)




* <u>Allergy</u>/hypersensitivity to CCBs

* Symptomatic <u>hypotension</u>  [[11]](/library/rOafFk)

* <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u>  [[12]](/library/7Oa4Fk)





### <u>Dihydropyridines</u>




* <u>Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy</u> (<u>HOCM</u>)  [[13]](/library/sOatFk)

* Severe stenotic <u>heart valve</u> defects  [[11]](/library/rOafFk)[[14]](/library/tOaX8k)[[15]](/library/GOaBFk)





### <u>Nondihydropyridines</u> [[16]](/library/uOap8k)




* Preexisting cardiac conduction disorders 

* <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</u>  [[17]](/library/up0prS)

* <u>Sick sinus syndrome</u>

* <u>Systolic dysfunction</u> (in <u>congestive heart failure</u>)

* <u>Bradycardia</u>

* <u>2° AV block</u>/<u>3° AV block</u>

* Combination with <u>beta blockers</u>: risk of <u>AV block</u>, <u>bradycardia</u>, and/or decreased cardiac contractility





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Nondihydropyridine CCBs</u> should not be combined with <u>beta blockers</u> because CCBs can enhance the negative <u>inotropic</u>, <u>chronotropic</u>, and <u>dromotropic</u> effects of <u>beta blockers</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Phenylalkylamines</u> (e.g., <u>verapamil</u>), which primarily affect the <u>calcium</u> channels of the <u>heart</u>, are contraindicated in cases of <u>heart failure</u> because of their negative effect on <u>myocardial contractility</u>.




We list the most important contraindications. The selection is not exhaustive.
